,t iN customary for public Journals, at the close of a year, to take a retrospective view of the events of that year. It does not become us, in this isolated corner ot the world, to contemplate the great occurrences which must form pages in the history ot Europe ; nor to otter any remarks on the civil war in the New World, which, no doubt, will rend a mighty Republic in twain. Our province is better confined to our own insular affairs, which, we venture to say, will mark an era in the political life of these distant Danish Colonies.

C 8 0 1. ft V U s.. þÿ common A danger produces þÿunanimity, it is said, and the progressive decay in the prosperity of this Island has, at least, verified the saying. An unusual interest in the affairs of the Island has been awakened during this year, now at its close. The complaint that there existed no public opinion seems on the point of being among the things that have passed away. The general desire for reforms, which the community long felt as necessary, but were timid to express, has, during this year, found an expression in the last Session of the Colonial Council. The st p ration of ! our finances from those of the mo.!: country, and, as a necessary consequence, seiflegislation in regard to them; the abolition of protective duties which have cramped the trade of the Island, and left competition no chance ; the promise of the blessings of a free press, which, however, should now have been in realization, þÿ these, and all collateral measures, springing from them, are among the matters in prospect which may be reckoned as peculiarly distinguishing the year of Grace 1861. These subjects, it is well to be remembered, are not the desires of a man, or a f w mm as has been declared, but we are confident in saying, they are the desiri s of nine-tenths of those with intelligence enough to comprehend their value. The recent elections go far to prove our assertion. Not one individual, known to be opposed to them, has been elected ; on the contrary we find that one individual, a talented man, received hut one single

vote through his unpopularity on tins very ground. But while we thus congratulate the public on having gained so much, we still must remind them, that these measures are only in embryo, and have yet to he sifted and arranged, and if we are not watchful, they might he also smothered. We must be awake and doing. Leave not all the labor to our representatives. Convoke public meetings, and by your petitions prove to the to mother-country in future, its desire grant ns whatever that, we may demand, if we could only unite to demand something, shall not be wanting an occasion of being gratified. When we thus prove ourselves capable ot selfgovernment, we will not tail to obtain it ; and then only will we experience, what we wish our renders, a happy and prosperous neir year.

AMERICAN NEWS. . Through the extreme kindness of Ilis Excellency the Governor, New placed in possession of the we have been N ork Daily Tribune of the 18th inst. Nothing new had taken place at Fort Pickens since the bombardment. The Connecticut, on her

way to New York, had touched at Tybee Island and Port Royal, and gathered some important News which, the Tribune says, it is not thought best to give the particulars of it. It however declares that it is probable that both Savannah and Charleston will soon be in the possession of the Federal troops. The Europa, with the þÿQueen s messenger, Capt. Seymour, on board arrived at Boston on the 17th inst. He left for Washington the same afternoon. Within 30 minutes after the Europa touched at Halifax, the British steam sloop-ot-war Rinaldo, lying in port, got up steam and left, in pursuance of some orders, it is supposed, brought by the Queen's messenger, to communicate with the Admiral of the British North American squadron. The British Mail steamship Africa had been detained by Lord Lyons to take despatches to his Government. She was however to have left on the 20th inst. In the House of Representatives, the Mason-Slidell affair was, on the 17th, under discussion. Mr. Cox (Ohio) was of the opinion that the United states naval officers were right in overhauling the Trent. He hoped that the action of the House of Representatives at least toward Powers will show a #wise and just conciliation, without any timid or time-serving concession. NIr. Yallandighani (Ohio) predicted that in less than three months Messrs. Slidell and Mason will be returned. Mr. Cox hoped the prediction would prove untrue. Mr. Diven (New York) was for leaving the question with England in the hands of

those on the United þÿStates part who will conduct the negotiation. It should be conducted with dignity and a due regard to its honor and interests. Under those circumstances he was willing to risk the chances of war. Two classes would he disappointed by tiie preservation of peace, namely, those who want a war to give strength to the Rebels and enable them to i succeed, and those who have been reveling in the spirit of bravado. 'The Tribune observes that the fiercest advocates of. war with England at all hazards, the noisiest blusterers about the American eagle and the British lion, are men who have long been suspected of being rebels at heart. Those who heartily wish the rebellion pul down are not anxious to precipitate hostilities.

CROIX þÿ þÿ -- þÿ þÿ address of Governor Hincks to the Legisfrom the Barbados Globe, in which copy lative Council of St. Lucia, which we will be found a statement of some of the difficulties in the way of Coolie Immigration to the British West India Colonies, and which will give our readers some idea . of the yet greater difficulties that will be placed in the way of an immigration of that class of labourers to this colony, when our Government begins to treat with the British Government on the subject. We have not heard the result of a meeting which has been held at Governmenthouse on the question of Immigration, but a preference seems to be pretty generally given to Chinese labourers for this Island, as being connected with less difficulty in obtaining them, and in their amalgamating more readily with our native labourers.

From the Barbados Globe, October 10, 1861. At a Meeting of the Legislative Council of St. Lucia, held on Tuesday, 1st instant, IlisExcellency F. Hincks, Esq., Govcrnorin-Chief, who arrived there on the 26th ultimo presided, and addressed the Board as follows : þÿ þÿ Honourable Gentlemen , þÿ chief My object in convening this mectmg of the Legislative Council lias been to submit tor your consideration a measure for

S; T. M 0 U « Yy II 1 amending the Ordinances providing fer the introduction, regulation, and government of | Coolie agricultural labourers. þÿ 1 have received a despatch from Her þÿMajesty s Principal Secretary of State for the Colonies, informing me that His Grace is so little satisfied with the working of the Immigration system in St. Lucia, during the year 1860, as disclosed in the various despatches, reports, and returns which have engaged his consideration, that lie shall consider it his duty to prohibit the shipment of any Coolies to this Colony, beyond those which may he brought by the ship already ordered, until he shall learn from me that the system now at work has been amended, on the points on which it is defective. þÿ It must lie obvious that the interests of the employers of labour in this Colony would bo greatly promoted by the encouragement, or when necessary the enforcement, of habits of industry among the labourers. One of the principal causes to which the failure of the present svstern is to be ascribed, is the absence of proper medical care of the Coolies, at the early period of disease. In order to obviate the ignorance and neglect through which the labourers often wilfully deprive themselves of such care, great watchfulness on the part of the proprietors or their agents is indispensable, and the statistical returns afford satisfactory evidence that in many ! instances, and more especially in those in which the proprietors reside on their estates, complete success has been the result.

The sickness and mortality have been light and the labourers iiave earned wages fully adequate to their wants. The same returns, however, exhibit many failures. On some Estates the aggregate weekly earnings of the labourers have been less than one-half what they have been on others ; and whether this is to be ascribed to sickness or idleness, it is necessary to provide an efficient remedy. 1 have given my anxious and unremitting consideration to this question, since the first introduction of Coolie Immigrants into this Colony, and I have endeavoured to make myself acquainted with the systems which have been long in operation in the important Colonies of British Guiana and Trinidad, and with the improvements which have been from time to time introduced into those systems. I believe it to be essentially necessary that a more active Executive supervision should be exercised in | this Colony ; and 1 trust that you will concur with me in thinking that the time lias arrived when the important office of Immigration Agent should he put on a more efficient footing. It will he the duty of the Executive to take care that the Special Stipendary Justices are regular m their peri- ; odical inspections of the Estates on which ; Coolies are located, and that they shall not ! only redress any real grievances complained of by the labourers, but shall likewise adopt vigorous measures to enforce the regular performance of daily labour. 1 fully recognise the principle, that the employer is

entitled to a fair þÿday labour s (or a full þÿday s pay ; and I do not anticipate any difficulty in framing regulations that will give satisfaction on the subject of wages. It will I think be expedient to impose additional penalties on idleness, and to adopt means to prevent the labourers from absenting themselves from work, under the pretence of sickness. But no measure is of more importance than | the establishment of General Hospitals at the principal Towns. These hospitals will not supersede the necessity of attending to the medical care of the labourers on the Estates ; but they will afford mehns for giving prompt and effectual relief in all cases which in the opinion of the medical

practitioners may require hospital treatment. It is desirable that the responsibility for the Medical cure of the labourers should, in future, devolve on the Executive, and I am persuaded that this can be effected without imposing any additional burthen on the employers, except in those cases in which gross neglect has taken place. I earnestly recommend this important subject to your attention. It is one on which there can be no conflicting interests. The anxious desire of the Secretary of State is that a satisfactory system ol Immigration should lie established, and it must be t he interest of the proprietors, on whom the cost of immigration mainly devolves, that the labourers should enjoy health, and be in a position to earn sufficient wages to enable them to obtain proper sustenance.

THE JOINT INTERVENTION IN 1IEX ICO. The Morning Pott, on authority aptreaty parently, between states that the terms of the the Queen, the Emperor of the French, and the Queen of Spain, are in course of arrangement for an immediate intervention, by the combined forces of the three Sovereigns, in the affairs of Mexico. The Allied Powers, it seems, have no intention of wasting powder and shot by waging a territorial war upon Mexico. The intention of the Allies, on the contrary, is to send a combined naval force into the Gulf of Mexico. This force will blockade, and it is apprehended, temporarily occupy, the principal ports upon the Gulf, such as Vera Cruz, Tampico, and one or two others. The plan on which they have agreed for the satisfaction standing claims is this: þÿ þÿ ot the out- TheAllied Powers will sequestrate the Customs revenues of the ports in question. They will charge their consuls, or some other authorities, jointly to collect these revenues at the different ports; and these consuls, acting together, will form a sort

T.. c B 0 I. X V I: S , of international commission, constituted for the purpose at each port. No ship will be able either to enter or clear at the ports of Vera Cruz, Tampico, &.C., without the authority of these consuls, who will exact þÿ and not only exact, but themselves also receive þÿ the Customs dues on such entrances and clearances. We believe that the Allies will retain about 50 percent, of these, and will pay over 50 per cent, to Mexico. Their j respective consuls, after paying over to the Mexican Government its share ot the proceeds, quarter by quarter, will divide the balance, or other half, rateably between the three countries. This arrangement will lie permanent, or will endure at least until all claims shall have been discharged. A ship ol war or two in the roadsteads ot each ot these ports will meanwhile secure the maintenance of the authority of the allied consuls. 'flie Patrie contradicts the report that the present state of Mexico is about to be the subject of a convention between the three Powers most interested in the question. The Patrie admits that the French Government has fully approved the conduct of its Minister in Mexico ; j that it has. expressed its great dissatis- faction with the measures ot the President Juarez, and its intention to protect the French interests affected by them. But no decision has been made as to the means to be employed to effect this result.

A correspondent of the New York Herald <rives the following account of the negotiations with Garibaldi: þÿ þÿ can I give you some very interesting particulars in regard to the proposition of Garibaldi to join our army, and the probability of his soon entering into the service of the United States. Nearly two months ago our Consul at Genoa wrote to Garibaldi on the subject of our civil war. Garibaldi promptly replied, saying that he 1 sighed tor retirement, but if the great cause of Republican Government, self-government, tree institutions þÿ which is the same throughout the world þÿ was at stake,' he might be induced to relinquish his long-cherished hope of withdrawal Consul and he begged the from public life, to express to our Government his deep sympathy in this hour of trial. He concluded his letter with the significant inquiry whether this conflict would result in the emancipation of the slaves? This correspondence was forwarded by our Consul to Secretary Seward, who communicated the same to the President. Mr. Lincoln immediately directed the Secretary of State to tender to Garibaldi, in the name of the President, the appointment of if Major-General rican Army, he would take a part in in the Amethis great contest. Mr. þÿSeward s reply to Garibaldi, addressed to our Consul at Genoa, rs one of the most elaborate, studied, and ornate pieces of rhetoric that has ever emanated from his pen, and will be admired when it conies to be published by the lovers of rhetoric

throughout the world. It was so general in its terms, arguing the point often presented to our readers, that if Republican Government fails here there is no hope for it anywhere else ; but as the Government at that time had no policy in regard to the confiscation and freeing

of the slaves of rebels, and the Secretary of State did not know whether the Government would adopt a policy on that subject, he dodged þÿGaribaldi s main and important question, and made no allusion to it whatever. But now that General Fremont has made a policy for the Government on this vexed question þÿ in full harmony with Garibaldi's views þÿ the friends of the Italian Liberator are sanguine that he will soon be here to accept the proffered commission in our þÿarmy. The Unit a ltaliana of Milan states that as soon as it became known that efforts were being made by the United States to obtain the services of Garibaldi, the following address was immediately covered with thousands of signatures: þÿ þÿ General, þÿ Do not goto America. The people have faith in you, and you must have faith in the people. The unity of Italy is far from being accomplished. You have laid its most solid foundation; you alone can complete your work. THE WAR IN MONTENEGRO. The Constitutional Correspondence of Vienna lias the following intelligence from Montenegro: þÿ þÿ The war in this place and in the Ilerzagovine is waged with great ferocity by both Christians and Turks. A thousand Albanian Catholics have brought to Soutari 29 heads of victims killed at Podgorizza. Abdt Pacha, the Governor, at first refused to pay them the usual premium, but, intimidated by their threats, he at last gave them 5,000 piastres. The requisitions made by the Turkish troops concentrated to act against Montenegro assume enormous proportions. For instance, the foukara (Mussulman peasants) in the districts of Vojnie, Travnik, and Vlasanilsa, are ordered to supply two million okas (2,564,000 kilos.) of barley, and 110 horses. The Turks, called out for military service, have mutinied at Krawesh and Grahovae, but they were at last taken to Mostar. Circulars have been addressed to the chiefs of districts, calling for new levies of bashi-bouzouks, to be immediately sent to the llerzegovine. The sandjak of Bihac is to supply 620 foot and 600 horse. Many

Christians who had already j)aid to he exonerated from the service, have been forcibly enrolled. Another circular from the Vizir demands 400 purses (80,000 fr.), and 800 okas of lard from the district of Vakil þÿf. A Dispatch from Kagusa of the 10th states that the advanced guard of the Turkish army, which had reached Zubzi, in the direction Of Sutorina, and Zaslap, towards Grahovo, on the road leading to Cettingne, for a distance of about 20 kilometres (124 miles), fell hack during the 16th and 17th on Trcbigne and Klohick. This measure appeared to have been caused by a hold movement of the insurgents under the famous mountain chief Luca Vucalowich. The Scrdar, Omcr Pacha, at the latest dates, was concentrating his troops at Trcbigne, which he makes his base of operations, and has strongly fortified it. The Vladika of Montenegro had got all his contingents under arms, and was awaiting the approach of the Turkish army on his territory. Omcr Pacha made a strong reconnaissance from Trehigne on the 21st inst., and ascertained that the Montenegrins had thrown up redoubts before Grahovo, but had made no preparations for assuming the offensive.

Soldiers Walking on þÿWater A letter from Paris þÿsays: þÿ The military preparations of the French Government are going on with great activity. Experiments arc just now going on at Vincennes with a view to use common rifled howitzers as mortars, by fixing them at a very sharp angle, which enable small shells to be thrown some six thousand metres. But these experiments excite but little attention in comparison with a new invention which has been tried with perfect success, and by which a foot soldier in heavy marching order is enabled to walk on the water without sinking. It consists of a pair of india-rubber boots and trousers, all of one piece, which are tilled with air a little below the waist, and heavily weighted at the feet. With these trousers on a detachment has frequently crossed the lake of Vincennes, where the water is about 15 feet deep, firing their muskets, and loadingas they went. The men sink about two feet, the water barely the top of their thighs, and appear reaching not to have any difficulty in keeping their balance and moving alone. The experiment is to be repeated in presence of the Emperor, and there is not the slightest doubt of its being adopted for the army. The consequence of the adoption of this system need hardly be pointed out. Fancy on a calm day at sea how easy it would be to lead three or four thousand men, who would forthwith walk ashore, and secure a landing for the rest of the force. For the crossing of a river the advantage of

this system is still more obvious, and the delays caused by the necessity for constructing bridges or discovering fords would be done away with. The Editor of the St. Croix Avis, Sir, Allow me as one who feels an interest in the success of any scheme having for its object immigration on an efficient scale, to express my dissent from your remarks in the paper of 18th instant on Governor þÿMinks address in St. Lucia. As I read those remarks before the address itself, 1 certainly felt considerable uneasiness at þÿ the difficulties in the way af Coolie Immigration to the British West India Colonies and the yet greater difficulties that will be placed in the way of an immigration of that class of laborers to this colony, when our Government begins to treat with the British Government on the þÿsubject. I was therefore most agreeably surprised, when by perusal a of the document itself, I found the en- j couraging opinion I had previously entertained on the subject of Coolie immigration

so far from containing any views or sen- Danish colonies in particular, on the contrary, by the great stress it lays on particular conditions for the assent of the British Government to Coolie immigration, entitles us to hope, that the peculiarities of our case will prove a most effectual circumstance in our favor, The subject held forth most prominently by Governor Hincks against the planters of St. Lucia, as the reason for prohibiting further importations of Coolies is the want of all systematic regulations for providing the labourers

with medical treatment and care, the very subject to which jointly with the regulations for the instruction of the þÿlabourers children, we have a right to point as honorable characteristics of our own system. That so striking a requisite as proper medical treatment of the immigrant laborers should be in an especial manner the object of the British Governþÿment s olicitude, is however no more than was to he expected ; hut what 1 consider as still more encouraging for our expectations of a favorable result of the active steps now known to he taken for either Coolie or Chinese emigration, are the remarks made by Mr. lliucks on the necessity of enforcing a proper quantity of work from the labourers. It has been long well-known to every one having a tolerable acquaintance with W est Indian affairs, that the chief cause of the ill success, or let us hope that we may now begin to have the right of saying the chief cause of the tardy success, of emancipation has been the fatal illusion, that the principles of government proper to a population having enjoyed personal and political liberty in many generations, must and should be applied in their full extent to a country just emerged from slavery. In these colonies an attempt was made to moderate the consequences of the abolition of slavery by reserving a certain amount of control over the emancipated people, so as to compel them to steady labour (unfortunately exempting the class least deserving it, viz. the emancipated slaves

in the towns) Although we here are on the whole pretty well agreed as to the beneficial results of this policy, only differing as to its extent and duration, we have always been under the impression, that it was considered inconsistent with English notions of freedom, to compel a man to work, who preferred starvation for himself and those by nature dependent upon him. There are not a few signs, that in England and in the English Colonies those first impressions have for some time been considerably modified, hut we have with pleasure the following enunciations of common sense and sound justice made by the Governor on this occasion. þÿ They (the Special Stipendiary Justices) shall not only redress any real grievances complained of I y the labourers, but shall likewise adopt vigorous measures to enforce tlic regular performance of daily labour." þÿ I fully recognize the principle, that the employer is entitled to a fair þÿday s labour for a full þÿday p s ay ; and I do not anticipate i any difficulty in framing regulations that ges trill give þÿ satisfaction on the subject of wa- It will, i think, he expedient to impose additional penalties on idleness, i and to adopt means to prevent the labourers from absenting themselves from j It was for our I work under the acting pretence of þÿsickness. on the principles very much strengthened by i here expressed, that twelve years ago the whole tenor of the discourse, which | Messrs. Gurney and Alexander thought proper, after a visit of a few days to this

timents averse to Coolie immigration to ; island, to represent the slate of things the W. I. colonies generally or to the ! here as being not far distant from slavery, and it is the clear evidence lying ir. Governor þÿHincks address, of a very different manner of judging W. I. relations among Englishmen, that relieves us from any fears, perhaps still lurking among us, as if our regulations were repugnant to English feelings, which I look upon as a most satisfactory circum stance, with regard to our own case. 1 remain, \rour obdt. servt. The annual examination of the Moravian School at Friedenstlial took place on Friday the 18th inst., in the presence of a large concourse of parents and friends, and gave general satisfaction. The children went through their different exercises in an orderly and proper manner, thereby reflecting great credit on their teachers who have, to all appearance, used their best endeavors in training and instructing them. The different kinds of needle work exhibited deserve praise. From the manner in which instruction is imparted to the children in this school it would be highly desirable that a higher class should be established into which the more advanced of the children could be drafted and receive instruction in the higher branches of education. The advantages of obtaining cheap Hooks &.c. possessed by the Reverend Inspector and the creditable manner in which both Children and Teachers acquitted themselves on this occasion, have caused these observations. Our correspondent þÿ I L . þÿ would do us a wrong if he should ascribe the remarks in our last on Governor þÿHincks address, as being dictated by a spirit hostile to Coolie Immigration. In stating that, in the address would be found some of the difficulties in the way of Coolie Immigration to the British West India Colonies, we pointed simply to the statement that Her Majesty's Secretary of State for the Colonies is so little satisfied with the working of the Immigration system in St. Lucia, that he considers it his duty to prohibit the shipment of any Coolies to that colony. Now if the Secretary of State, after having allowed the emigration of Coolies to Her Muj þÿesty scolonies should afterwards find fault with the working of the system, we see in the fact a tendency in the British Government to exercise a very severe scrutiny into the working of that system anywhere, hut, as we may suppose, more especially in foreign countries. As our regulations may be supposed to l>e unknown to that Government we can readily conceive that a length of time will transpire before negotiation might set matters to right. Of course, it remains to be seen whether the British Government will take the same favorable view of our regulations, especially the Labour Act, as our correspondent docs.

With this conviction the Danes are just now impatient of further negotiation, and even desirous of settling the Schleswig and Holstein question by a stand-up fight with Prussia. It may seem a little amusing that a nation which , with all its dependencies, can scarcely make up two and a quarter millions which lias an army under 10,000 men, and a revenue of about a million aud a quarter, should bo anxious to enter into mortal combat with Piussia. Prussia boasts that she can with an effort bring 500,000 men into the field, aud that she has a population

now advancing to twenty millions. Yet Denmark is quite iu earnest iu desiring to go to war with her. It looks like David challenging Goliah. Tho match, however, is not quite so unequal as it appears. If Denmark has only 10,000 men to oppose to fifty times as many, Denmaik has a fleet, and Prussia lias none. Piussia could easily pour her armies through the Duchies of Luuenburg and Ilolstcin and Schleswig, which, with Jutland, make up the peninsula which is all that the Danes have of mainland. This is the Danish view, founded upon tho chauces of war, aud upon the assumption that Prusaia sooner or later will certainly attack them. There is no doubt that Prussia, as the representative of Germany, is the aggressor in this matter. The most despotic of German Princes grievances pretend to of be seaudal zed by the constitutional Holstein. Every concession on the part of Denmark is treated as an admission that she was always in tho wrong. siaos to raise a fleet, and they are also boasting that the object of the fleet is to coerce Denmark. It is this which makes ti e Danes so impatient to settle the quarrel at once. The present possessions otthut country are by no means more than sufficient to enable her to maintain her independence among the Powers of the North ; and, if Prussia strips her of tho dependencies she holds by treaty, and some of which, indeed, Prussia sold atrd received an equivalent for, this Power, which can so ill be spared, must fall to nothing. Whatever may be the pretence, no one can mistake the tea object ; and it seems to us that if our Government interposes advice in such a crisis, it should he that all matteis in dispute he at once brought to diplomatic issue and settled definitely. If Prussia is really aiming herself to fight Denmark at sea, she is doing a most shortsighted thing. There is no country in Europe more interested in keeping the peace than Prussia, llcr existence depends upon the general conservative

feeliDg of Europe in favour of things as they are. Surely it is not for her to agitate against the Danes in defence of the cause of nationalities. Her Polish subjects might come forward in answer to sueh a summons, and push the princiare indignant and quite ready to fight, ple to inconvenient const quences. The but Danes it is not from them that danger is to be dreaded to the peace of Europe. Of course, they are only desirous to be lot alone. We hope, however, that Prussia herself will think twice before she attacks them. We have no wish to be put to our election of supporting her with all our power or of seeing her become a prey to a strong neighbour. Yet this is likely to be the end had any war which Prussia may begin. She of much better extend the blessings of a real Constitution to her own people than remodel the Holstein Budget by force of aims. She is not too strong either at home or abroad. She is too cold and pedantic to feel or inspire any such warmth of friendship as would incline us to stand by her even in her follies and her errors. When wo wish her well and desire her to be strong, it is rather from policy than from any special sympathy between our nature and hers. 26th October 1861. To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis, Sir, To keep the public informed of bow matters are progressing in St. þÿJohn Church, s under the j clever rectorship of Mr. Almon, I beg to mention that on Sunday, 20th inst., bis audience in the pews did not amount to sixty persons, and altogether in the church, to about one hundred and fifty persons. Last evening he held service and about sixty individuals attended, making an offering not amounting to (from all appearances) one dollar; the church requiring, at present, an expenditure of at least two dollars for lights, for the evening I am of opinion that Profit and Lots account in the church books, will not long hence show a balance on the left quarter , or, to prevent which, the incumbent and the remnant of his vestry, will have to exercise their financiering abilities to a great extent!!! Doubtless, by applying to the right quarter, the finances will bo improved? When we now take into consideration that the congregation of St. þÿJohn Church s amounts to about six thousand persons, fifteen hundred of whioh number are communicants, you will he in a position to form an idea to what a pitiable state tho parish is reduced, and what the amount of dissatisfaction with the rector Mr. Almon must be, when so small a percentage of the congregation, can be induced to attend

divine service held by him ; the more so when wo bear in mind the large number of communicants in that parish. To such a state of degeneracy matters in St. þÿJohn Church s have never (in the memory of some of the oldest inhabitants) fallen, and, 1 fear, we will still further have to deplore tho fate of this seot, unless another incumbent bo shortly appointed, who could have the confidence and respect of the congregation aud restore' the pure faith of the Church of England, in this, at present, unfortunate parish. I am dear Sir, Yours Respectfully, Observer St. Croix, Basin 24th October 1861.

Twelfth Meeting. Concluded. The 1st member for Christiansted (Arnesen j defended the amendments of the Committeelie considered the proposal to appoint 2 Government-secretaries instead of one as not advisable. It would bo a wroDg step to create two posts instead of one, at the very time when wo wauted just as much a reduction in the 'number of officials as of expenses. To demand tho appointment of 2 officials instead of one, each at a lower salary, was very much like saying that the standard of the men required had been lowered. Ho would as an illustration of what he meant, observe, that the island of Barbados had a Governor and a colonial secretary without any officially appointed secretariat, but merely with a few clerks employed by him. It had been said in favor of the proposed 2 secretaries, that, as His Excellency the Governor, who was responsible for the Government, bad recommended their appointment, it ought not to be opposed. Now, he for his part did not acknowledge the responsibility of the Governor; his power was so limited that his responsibility could not be very great. He would also oppose any increase of salary for the Lutheran Clergyman in Frederiksted. The Committee had likewise urged that the business of the Custoin-hou-e was not more than could bo dono by the preseot stall', and that tho expenditure ou this bead ought to be kept down. He could not see how the repeal of 6 11 a of the Law of 30th Juno 1850 could cause an increase of labor to tho Custom-hou.-o officials ; and he

would vote against the amendment and subameudmeut of the Governor ad II B. b. 4. By tho time that clause was repealed a new Colonial Council would very likely exist, and there would be plenty of lime then to make such arrangements as might be required. Ho could understand that the out-door work of the Custom-house might bo increased by tho change, and when it did take place tho requisite sum might bo voted. The Governor directed the þÿCouncil sattention to the fact, that the proposal relating to the appointment of 2 Government-Secretaries, would not, as was stated by the last speaker, cause any increase of the present number of Officials, just as little as any increase of the present expenses. The proposal bad only for object, to divido the business which now devolved both on tho Government-Secretary and on the Chef de bureau, jointly, between 2 Government-Secretaries, and to divido the present amounts of salaries in another manner. With regard to tho increase of business for tho subordinate officials at the Custom-houses, which would be caused by the eventual adoption of the Draft of a Custom-Law, proposed by tho members of the Committee, ho stated that, a3 far as regarded goods imported from tho Mothcrcountry iu danislr vessels, at present special investigation was only made at tho Customhortscs hero of transit goods imported here uu-

der Seal and on wliicli goods half duty, according to 6 II b of the Law of 30th June 1850, was now collected ; þÿ whereas no such special investigation was made with regard to those goods, whether tlie production of the Mothercountry or goods that had paid duty there, which were imported here free of duty when accompanied with a Customhouse- Certificate from the Motbercountry, in accordance with 6 II a of the above quoted Law. A repeal of this exemption from duty for the lastinentioned goods, as proposed in 1 of the abovemeiitioned Draft, would naturally render a special investigation of these goods just as necessary as with regard to all other goods on which duty had to be paid. If it even was to be supposed, that the importation from the Motbercountry of the goods treated of here and comiug under the head of those mentioned in 0 II a of the Law of 30th June 1850, the value of which could at present be estimated at about $180,000 p. a., would decrease should the exemption fiom duty', be repealed, such a decrease would materially be counterbalanced by a corresponding increase of the importation from other places, and the increase in the business of the Customhouse Officials would he just the same. The 1st member for Frcderikstcd (Sarauw) maintained that it ought to be left to the Governor to regulate the division of labor in the þÿSecretary s Office. He considered the sums hitherto voted for Customhouse expeuses sufficient. It was principally owing to the faults

of the tariff, that the work in the Customhouse was increased. Concerning the increase proposed in the Lutheran þÿClergyman s alary in þÿi rederiksted he would, as already stated, vote for it on the condition, that he was bound to perform such rites as the Clergymen of other denominations refused to do. He would nevertheless vote for the amendment of the Committee, which course he did not think contradictory. The Clergyman might send in accounts to Government for his travelling expenses. The 1st member for Christiansted (Arnoscn) spoke again against the appointment of 2 secretaries. The purpose of this new arrangement was evidently merely to givo the same persons now employed an increase of salary. If the object was to obtain the services of a man of eminent qualities, then $2,800 would not even be a sufficient salary. His Excellency the present Governor ought to know that better than any one else. lie begged to recall to his momory the attempt made by a certain party which he would designate as that of the þÿ þÿscribes, to lower the salary, he was in the receipt of when Government secretary, and with how much indignation the attempt was received. He could still not see what was to be gained by the appointment of 2 secretaries. The 5th member for Christiansted (Kothe) remarked that it was not so easy to get eminent men from Copenhagen to come out here. Ho thought the appointment of the 2 secretaries, as proposed by the Government, preferable to having a government-secretary as hitherto, who

had been a sort of irresponsible Vice-Governor. The Governor ought to bo the sole responsible person. The division would effect a saving of labor. It was, as he had remarked, above quito uncertain whether acolonial secretary of the kind described by the Committee was obtainable. The 4th Crown member (Ussing) thought that the question of the proposed addition to the lutheran þÿclergyman ssalary had taken a wrong turn. It was not, as some members seem to think, a question of, whether ho was to perform the rites, that other clergymen refused to perform, but whether he should be enabled to attend efficiently to his own work. It was admitted, that it was desirable that there should be a lutheran clergyman in Frcderikstcd. If so, it was necessary that the salary should be such as to induce capable men to accept the office. It was alreatty accompanied with considerable difficulty to obtain proper candidates even for far better livings here than the one in Frederikstcd. The 1st member for St. Johns ('Elliott) thought it strange that, whereas able olorgymen of other persuasions could maintain themselves and families without stato support, tho lutheran clergyman, in despite of such support, required still greater support. f The 1st member for Christiansted f Arnesen) agreed with Elliott

The 1st member for Clnistinnsted (Arnesen) begged the permission to ask His Excellency tho Governor, if he was able to inform the Council what had been tho fate of the proposal for extending the Danish law of the press to the Colonics, that had been adopted in the last session. Free Trade and the French Colonies The new commercial system granted by France toiler colonies of Martinique, Guadaloupe, and the Isle of Reunion, superseding the former prohibitive regulations, came into forco in the begiuning of last month. By this change the above islands are opened to the commerce and navigation of the whole world. The importation of merchandise will take place on the same terms as into France, except where tho colonial tariff' is more liberal, in which case the latter rate is retained. Trade can be carried on under any flag, but, with certain exceptions, a differential duty Is charged on foreign as

compared with Frincli ships. All export duties on colonial merchandise are abolished. English vessels will now bo enabled to tube cargoes of foreign goods to these islands, and return laden with produce, either to tlieir port of shipment or to France. The production of sugar is expected to be largely benefited, and increased activity is also looked for iu tbe coffee, dye woods, and spirit trades. The piincipal articles imported by tbe three islands arc wood for building, manufactured iron, salted meat and fish, butter, oil, flour, and coal, and at each colony there is a port offering every convenience to maritime commerce. The change
nearly approaching free trade appears to bo tho attempted by i commencement of a þÿ new and important era for ropean Times , October 17.

EXTRAC T OF THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE BUR- GHER COUNCIL OF ST. CROIX. On Thursday 26th September 1861 at noon a meeting of the Rurgher Council 1 was held at Government House, as appointed by Ilis Excellency the Governor, in order to consider a proposition from a number of planters for importation of Eastindia Coolies. Tbc members of the Council were present, excepting Mr. H. C. Ratcliffe, who bad reported to be unable to attend : Mr. R. Knight met, being elected the day before. Also were present Chamberlain Rothe and Judge Stakcmann, at the request of the Governor. The Governor communicated the purport of the petition received, and after explaining the state of the case, observed that the first question would be, if the Council would alter the resolution come to in October last year, that the Council should take no further steps as to the importation of Coolies, but only contribute $30 for each Coolie eventually imported, leaving any further arrangements to tbc importers and to Government. It would thereafter have to be considered, if the terms for contracts with Coolies, as proposed, should be agreed to, as basis for a convention with the British Government. Mr. Arnesen observed, that the question about Coolies to be imported on terms different from those recommended by the Burgher Council in October 1860, could of course always be reconsidered,

whenever, as in the present instance, new proposals were laid before the Council. lie stated bis view, that under the circumstances now ascertained, it would be far preferable to obtain an importation of Chinese, who always can be had, and who are considered to be more industrious than the ordinary Coolies ; the importation of them would be a simple mercantile business, not depending on the uncertain consent and objectionable control of a foreign government; there being no obligation to return the Chinese, after the expiration of their contracts, to their own country (as would be the case with the Coolies after 5 years) at the expense of the public, and no occasion for new salaries from the Landtreasury for a British consular agent and a superintendent, he considered it likely, that Chinese immigration

1 ® g B Qj (! X would also be cheaper, as well as more reliable, than that of East India Coolies. He also observed on the consequences to the estates, of introducing into this Island such a system of þÿ as stipulated for the Coolies now in St. Kitts. Mr. Newton replied to the statements of Mr. Arnesen, and especially insisted on the probability of obtaining E. J. Coolies in a much shorter time, than Chinese. After further opinions being given both by the Governor and by the gentlemen present, Mr. Newton proposed : That the Burgher Council of this Island withdraw the resolution of 10th October 1860, and recommend to His Excellency the petition signed by several planters (representing twothirds of the taxpayers), regarding Immigration and woultl respectfully beg, that be should take it into bis immediate consideration þÿ and forward the documents to Copenhagen. Mr. Arnesen, observing on the extent of the documents and the very imperfect acquaintance of both subscribers and members with the details therein contained, proposed as an amendment: þÿ That the case be postponed for further discussion by tbc Burlier Council in a meeting on Monday þÿnext. The amendment was negatived by 4 voles against 2; and Mr. þÿNewton p s roposition carried by 4 votes against 2; Mr. Arnesen and Mr. Heyliger reserving their dissent. The Governor stated, that lie would do his best to forward the case to Copenhagen by next þÿday mail. s The meeting thereafter was closed.

BY SINCLAIR TO! SLY. We are in a rebellion, or insurrection of extraordinary magnitude. Common consent attributes it to the existence of Slavery. The cause beiDg removed, the disease dies. The removal of a darn allows the free course of the stream Remove the dam of Slavery from the broad river of the Union, and the puro waters of Freedom will speedily wash this foul scum of Rebellion into the great gulf of the Past. Slavery, however, is, in the opinion of many well-meaning people, a constitutional disease, to be removed ouly by a remodelling of that instrument to suit the new condition of the political patient. The honest scruples of these persons must be respected. Another large class assert that the disease is not constitutional, but

S; T, C Bad k V; (, S , in violation of that law of national life, aud that all our political diseases arise from such violation. The opinion of these people are abo entitled to attention, and however they may difler from the, former on these matters, all agree that, had there been no Slavery iu the South, there would have been no rebellious attempts to overthrow the Government and exteud þÿ the þÿinstitution. This is the common platform on which all stand, one of its planks being a desire to end this rebellion and establish peace with honor to the Government and the people. So far so good. Another plank in this political structure is the admission that Emancipation would end the rebellion at once and effectually. '1 be fiist named parties, that is to stly, those who believe that the Constitution protects Slavery, are loth to adopt this coutse so long as there is any possibility of otherwise crushing the rebellion, hut are willing to resort to this remedy it nothing else will cure the disease. I would willingly address a few words to this class Many of the wisest and best men whom our country has ever produced, deny most emphatically that s the Con- stitution protects or even recogniz Slavery, hut for the present purpose let it be admitted that it does both recognize and protect tint institution. Now, it is a principle of law, as well as of comtnon-sei.s o and common justice, that those who violate the law, !o by such acts forfeit their right to enjoy tin? privileges the law guarantees to those who obt y its provisions,

Thus murderers, buigla s, forgers, or other criminals who transgress the law, forfeit their rights under it, and aro deprived ol their because ties, or it may be of their lives, simply liberthey have done unpardonable violence to the law ; and any attorney who should set up the plea that his murdering or thieving with having his legal rights inteifered client was by the gallows or the prison, would naturally deserve and gain the contempt of the community. Violators of law forfeit their claims to the rights guaranteed to those who obey it. If such violators continued to enjoy the same privileges in society as those who never offend, there would be an end to all law, and civilization be extinguished. Force would take the place of order, and the weak yield to the strong. The distinguishing trait of civilization is, that the weakest member of the community is, in the eye of the law, strong as the strongest; were it otherwise, there could be no civilization The South, or those living in tho Southern States, who have by their rebellion violated the Constitution, have forfeited their claims to its protection, and are now, in their relation to the Government, in the same society they have no legal or constitutional po.-ition þÿ as that of a convicted criminal toward rights left them, except the right of trial, and that trial is now going on from day to day in presence of the whole world, having Deity for the presiding Judge and humanity for the jury, and must he dealt with by Government as the

law and society deal with individual criminals. They must be punished for their than aud as these have been greater transgressions the transgressions of any single criminal, so in the punish- ment to be awarded mu>t be great proportion, and the severest that can be inflicted is to deprive them of that institution for the perpetuation of which, as their so styled V ice-President declares, they began the rebellion. Hence we may assume that it will bo right, proper, and efficacious to proclaim Emancipation throughout the rebellious States, and that such declaration will not, for tho reasons above given, be any violation of the Constitution or any infringement ot their legal tights. There arc many who admit the efficacy of ing þÿ Emancipation, but who of þÿ And why last 1 It is admitted invariably speak it as that timid and temporiz- þÿ a last þÿresort. this rebellion is purely and solely the work of the slaveholders. It is also admitted that the Government would be justified in proclaiming Emancipation þÿ as a last resort.' Allow me to ask what is meant by this 'last resort V If it is meant that when tho Government back'd up by the people of the loyal States, shall have tried by other means to crush this rebellion, and failing in all others, tlieD, and not till then Emancipation is to a be what is meant by þÿ last þÿproclaimed þÿ resort, allow me to if this is suggest that it is a most latnc and impotent þÿconclusion. Think. It is proposed to have Government do all it can by its armies, by
blockade, by non-intorcourse, by stopping mails, by fines, by imprisonment, etc., and tailing with

all these powerful aids to crush tho most wicked rebellion that ever cursed humanity, then Email cipatiou may bo proclaimed. The proclama tions of a Government thus defeated in its attempts to maintain its existence by putting down such a rebellion, would not bo worth the paper they were written on. IV/io would respect them ? Not those whom its armies could not conquer; not these whom its fines and imprisonment could not iutimidate ; not those whom it would, by proclamation, liberate. Why ? Because a Government thus weak, thus unable to maintain itself by enforcing its laws, would not have the power to make its proclamations respected. If such a proclamation is to be issued at all, now is the time, while the Government is strong, or has the credit of being strong enough to make its proclamation respected. Thus much for the scruples of the temporisers, and their willingness to use Emancipation as a þÿ last þÿresort. Let us now discuss a side-issue, and one that is often urged as au objection to Emancipation. I refer to the fear that a declaration of Emancipation would inaugurate a servile insurrection, and that a second act of tho St. Domingo Tragedy would be cnactel in our Southern States. But why should the slaves join in insurrection, and cut their þÿmasters throats, in face of the fact, that the Government had proclaimed Emancipation, and would in self-defence enforce such proclamation by its armies, just as it does and must euforce all its other acts ? The Government having pro-

men, would be no longer þÿ chattels personal claimed these slaves free, they then become þÿ, and being men, would ho entitled to the rights of citizens, and consequently to protection from Government. In enforcing this protection, Government might use these freed people themselves as instruments with which to execute its decrees, while at tho same time this very use of them implies the ability of Government to control them, and thus most effectually prevent all possibility of servile insurrections to on do the with the blacks, as it is now trying part of the more dangerous insurrection of their white masters. The true and ouly way forever to prevent all slave insurrections is to have no slaves to riser There wore no unusual or improper excitements when Emancipation took cllect in tho British West-Indies. There would bo none hero. As the hour drew near that was to set thousands of human beings free and transform them from mere chattels to human beings, every breath grew shorter, every pulse beat quicker, and catch eagerness to every ear listened with intense the first sound of that bell that was to proclaim þÿ Liberty throughout all the Land unto all tho inhabitants þÿthereof, and when its last echoes died away in the valleys of those beautiful islands, there arose such a shout of joy as never before found vent from human lips. So would it be in insurrection. cipation never begot our own South. Eman- That is the natural offspring of Slavery. I have thus disposed of the Insurrectionary

objections, aud will now consider the conceded rights of loyal slaveholders in the rebellious States, for it is admitted that they have rights whioh should bo respected. Let Government lay a tax on the whole people of the Confederacy, loyal and rebellious, and collect it, when laid, at the point of the bayonet if necessary, (and this, as a matter of pecuniary economy, would be better than to carry on a long war,) and pay these loyal men for their slaves. Let the same be done with tho border slave States, and thus by purchase from good citizens and by confiscation from rebellious ones, would bo established Universal Emancipation throughout our United States. I have thus argued the case up to tho establishment of Emancipation. 1 will now consider its influence as a means of crushing tho rebellion. Facts warrant the assumption, that this rebellion had its origin in, and is carried on for the sole purpose of extending and perpetuating slavery. All the orators of the South, all tho leaders of their public opinion, take this posi tion ; they even say that our present Constitution is good enough in every particular savo one, and that one defect in that great document is, that it docs not provide sufficiently for the extension, perpetuation and protection of slavery, and therefore, as they have not at the present time the political power to alter that instrument (in accordance with its provisions)

so as to suit it to their views, they resort to physical force ami cover their States with of groat armies, with the avowed determination destroying this Constitution and the Government founded on it, and thus making room for their own more perfect Slavery-making bondage-extending -document. This is their avowed object, patent to the world. Now, if we can by any means proper to use, put an end to this institution, will not such act put an end to this wicked rebellion ? If we effectually extinguish slavery in the rebellious States, and prohibit its future introduction there, will we not establish peace? If cause precedes effect, we will most assuredly. The rebels must lay down their arms, and submit to the laws when we have deprived them of the power (I assume that we have the power to enforee our Proclamation, and if we have not, wo are no longer a government) to coutiuue the existence of their institution, and thus we shall sec the positive influence of Emancipation as a means to crush the rebellion and establish peace. Let emancipation be proclaimed, and down goes the þÿSlaveholders Rebellion. Having thus established the position that Emancipation will crush out the insurrection, I will now consider its effects on the whites of both sections, South as well as North. I assume that there is a certain amount of labor to be done iu the Southern States, aud that the freed negroes, from experience aud aclimation, are the best qualified persons to perform that labor, aud

would be employed to do it under a system of wages, (instead of the lash,) prices being regulated by the laws of demand and supply. These negroes being thus paid for their work, would consume more of the products of white men employed in the mechanic arts ; more especially those products not absolutely necessary to life, as cheap ornaments, and those thousands of fancy articles that an uneducated people are so fond of, and which they always buy so freely in proportion to their moans. Rut it may be said, this system of wages would enhance the cost of the products grown by the labor of these people, and this increased cost would have to bo borne by the consumers of these products. If this were true, it would bo owing to the fact, that these black people free would get more for their labor than black people in bondage: and if this were so, then it would follow, that the freevelling up ing of these þÿ the people of labor to a price would have the effect of 'le- point where tho poor white men of those regions could afford to do it, a condition of things not heretofore existing in any slave State, tho rule there being, that the planter, who owns both capital and labor, can afford to do woik cheaper than the poor white, who merely owds his labor, which he wishes to sell, and can find no market tor, because ho cannot work as cheap as the black slave of the capitalist. Hence it is, that there arc so many of tho þÿ poor white trash' scattered all over the South. Emancipation, according to

this reasoning, (originated by the opponents of Emancipation,) would benefit the poor white most decidedly. The increased demand by tho freed blacks for products of the whites, both South and North, wou'd add greatly to the demand for tho labor of these whites, and thin Emancipation would benefit them pecuniarily, to say nothing of its removing the degradation now attached to labor in consequence of Slave ry. Whore there are no slaves, laboring men arc respectable and respected. Where Slavery exists, the laborer is neither. The New-England States illustrate the one condition, and the South the other. But, say some, if you emancipate the negroes they will not work ; tho stimulus of wages is not sufficient to induce them to labor. Well, grant that they will not. Suppose they choose to drag out a miserable, handto-mouth existence, as the poor whites of the South now do, and earn barely enough under tho pressure of starvation to support life ? What then ? If they refuse to work as regularly and efficiently as heretofore, w ill not their refusal make a demand for the labor of the poor whites of both sections, and thus materially help to draw off from the great cities of the North the surplus labor, now vainly seeking employment, aud thus greatly benefit those laborers 1 Such neglect to work by the freed negroes would have none other than a beneficial effect on tho poor whites, by giving them tho work that the free blacks refuse to do ; but if the freed blacks go on and work industri-
ously for wages, then their increased ability to consume would of necessity make an increased demand for the products of white men, now

5 T t £ 8i P l V I S t employed in the manufactures consumed by tho blacks. Thus emancipation, like all good deeds, would bring its own reward. I have thus endeavored to show that a proclamation of Emancipation would end the rebellion ; that its effects would be beneficial to the whites, and if my arguments are sound, let the þÿl eople, who make aud unmake administrations, demand of tho present Government an immediate Proclamation of Emancipation.

The Court of Policy met on the 9th inst., when the following Despatch from the Secretary of State, announcing the appointment of Mr. Hincks to the Government of this Colony, was read þÿ Copy. British Guiana. þÿ þÿ Sir, þÿ Downing-street, I have had the honour of sub- 3rd Sept., 1801. mitting to Her Majesty the name ol 3Ir. not work on an average one day in each

Hincks, now Governor-in-Chief of Barbados and the Leward Windward Islands, as a proper person to succeed Mr. Wodehouse in the important charge of the Government of British Guiana. þÿ Mr. Hincks has been instructed to notify to you the time at which you may expect that he will arrive to assume the Government. þÿ In notifying this appointment to the Court of Policy you will be pleased to state that Her þÿMajesty s Government have been anxious to secure for the Colony in the office of Governor, serexplain vices not less active and energetic than those which have been rendered by Mr. YVodehouse, adding that they are assured that Mr. Hincks will give his best efforts to promote the welfare and prosperity of the Colony, and to give effect to the policy of Her þÿMajesty Govern- s ment at all points with zeal and fidelity. þÿ I have, &.c , &c., þÿ (Signed) NEWCASTLE. þÿ Lieut. Governor Walker, The Despatch is highly complimentary to Mr. Hincks, and shews that His Excellency is held in high estimation at the Colonial Office. We understand that the new Governor will not be here until the end of the year, as Mr. James Walker, who has been appointed to succeed him in the Government of Barbados, will not be out to relieve him until that time. An impression exists in this Colony that Mr. Hincks is inimical to Immigration. It appears to have been produced by certain speeches delivered by Mr. Hincks at Barbados, and in London, and by Despatches to the Secretary of State, in which he dwelt at some length

on the labour question, and the results of emancipation. The view which he took of those questions was certainly very different from those entertained in this Colony; hut it should be remembered that Mr. Hincks spoke and wrote as the Governor of Barbados, where the labour question and the results of emancipation appear under a different aspect from that which they present in all the other West India Colonies. Barbados, in this respect, stands alone. The island is one of the most densely populated countries in the world, in proportion to its extent. The people there are compelled to work from sheer necessity. If a man will not in work neither shall lie eat is the law Barbados, where the condition of the labouring population is closely assimilated to that of the mother country. There a man is bound to work ; lie must earn his meal before he can eat it. Immigration is not required in Barbados, where there is already a redundant population. We do not see, therefore, in the views publicly enunciated by Mr. Hincks, anything opposed to Immigration in a Colony placed under different circumstances. British Guiana, unlike Barbados, has only a very sparse population, while the extent of its territory is sufficient to support more than ten thousand times the number of its present inhabitants. Here the labouring population are not under the same necessity to work, as the people of Barbados. None but those who are naturally inclined to be industrious work six days in the week ;

the rest of those employed upon estates work only from two to lour days, during which time they earn quite enough to satisfy their limited wants. The people who cultivate small plots of ground for themselves, work still less. They do

week throughout the year. Immigration in such a country is absolutely necessary to its existence. If the supply of labour derived from these sources were stopped, the whole of the estates would go out of cultivation ; trade, commerce, agriculture would he paralysed ; and every interest in the country would be ruined. We feel assured that Governor 11 nicks, when he comes to reside amongst n , will see these things as clearly as the colonist themselves; and that, so far from attempting to check the flow of immigration, he will do the utmost in his power to promote and increase it. Believing that our new Governor, who has exhibited an aptitude for business which has won for him the confidence of Her þÿMajesty s Government, will take a correct view of this question þÿ one of vital importance to this colony þÿ we think that all should suspend their judgment, until His Excellency has himself revealed the line of p'olicy which he intends to adopt. The Militia is fast becoming a public nuisance. The men are becoming disgusted with their parades, at which they make no progress in a knowledge of their drill. The Militia has been established about four years, and neither officers nor men know anything more of their duties now than they did three months after they were enrolled. This is attributable in part to the want of system, and in part to the officers, who have not been taught their duties, and will not take the trouble to learn them. There are one or two exceptions ; but,

as a general rule, the officers know nothing themselves, and consequently cannot instruct or drill the men. The men are naturally disgusted at being dragged out twice a week from their business, to blunder through movements that they ought to have thoroughly learnt four years ago. The New Militia Law relating to the collection of fines, by summoning the parties before the Police Magistrate, is now in operation. Many parties have been of summoned ready, and fined, some them heavily. al- We regret to see a disposition on the positions part of those who have been placed the of authority to exercise in power entrusted to them in a harsh and arbitrary manner. They like to carry things with a high hand ; but this demeanour is not likely to conciliate the men or to reconcile them to the performance of a very irksome duty. This soit of conduct may be carried too far ; and if officers do not know' how to behave as gentlemen, they may some day, when they least expect it, cease to be officers. þÿ Colonist.

(From the Illustrated London News, Oct. 12 ) The Attack of the llritiwh Embassy at Jeddo, Japan. Full details of the murderous and evidently premeditated attack on the members of the British Legation at Jeddo, on tin- 5th of July last, have been received. The details of the assault are dramatic and interesting. The party in the Legation had dined, Mr. Alcock had retired to rest, but some of the young gentlemen walked into the garden to look at that comet which paid us a visit in the summer. Hence they went to bed not a fall some of them did little later than usual, and asleep at once. T heir home was a temple, having a great door under a portico, but easily entered frum the garden in almost any part, full of intricate passages parti-

ally lighted, and rooms divided by a paper sliding iu grooves. Suddenly turious noise screens was heard at the great door. A servant of Mr. Consul Morrison saw a man clad in armour eater, and stealthily warned his master, handing him a revolver. Then a loud cry was heard. It came from Mr. Oliphant, who, carrying a heavy hunting-whip, had issued forth to chastise the midnight disturbers of the peace, and had encountered a man who cut him over the shoulder with a sword, and who was seconded by another scoundrel. While Mr. Oliphant kept them at bay with his whip, Mr. Morrison came up and shot one of the assasins dead; but his second ball glanced from the cuirass of the other, and the ruffians, plyiug their swords, wounded Mr. Morrison iu the head aud Mr. Oliphant in the wrist. As this crisis Mr. Bussell and Mr. Wirgman (the special artist of this Journal j arrived, aud the Japanese fell back into the darkness, cutting and slashing at posts and screens as they retired. -In the meantime Mr. þÿAloock room s had been sought out by the assassins, but, though these entered every other room in the place, they missed their way to his apartment Mr. Alcock joined the other gentlemen in the verandah. They were six in all, ouo disabled, and they mustered among them two revolvers and three swords. Nat far off they heard the crash of glass þÿ it was the work of the band seeking Mr. Alcock þÿ and every moment they expected to see the assassins rushing on. Not so ; the assassins had mistaken their way ; time

wasgiiued; the yacuuins, the arrived, and, falling upon or Japanese guard, assassins, killed five and drove the others away. There was a brief combat, in the garden, and then all was still , but the inmates of the house did not retire again to rest. They w itched all night with the Japanese soldiers, and only discovered in the grey of the morning how many of their assailants bad been destroyed. Measures were taken to prevent a second surprise by calling a up the ltingdove, aud placing on the premises guard of Frenchmen and marines. Mr. Alcock summoned the members of the other legations to meet him and take measures for their common security; and the Japanese Governor at Kaua- guard to the house of Consul Vyse, sent a guwa. The assault upon this unprotected abode of the representatives of the Queen iu Jeddo seems to have been well planned, and the whole of the occupants had a narrow escape Our Special Artist and Correspondent, several of whose Sketches of the attack upon the household of the British Consul-General at Jeddo appear in this þÿweek Impression, s gives his version of the outrage as follows : þÿ Yokuhama, July 11. I thought to have bccu enabled to send you by this mail some interesting sketches from tho interior of Japan, having como to this place overland from Nagasaki, but serious events have occurred at Jeddo, aud I therefore hasten to send you a slight account of what took place. We had only been in Jeddo two days, fatigued with our þÿmouth trip, s when, having retired

to rest about half-past ten p. in., wo were awoke by loud auu repeated knockiugs at tho front door. Thinking there was a fire, or some sli 'lit disturbance, wc at first took no notice of the noise, Jout in a short time the knocking became so loud as to resemble discharges of musketry, and tho shuffling of feet and rushing about aroused us thoroughly. Presently two pistol shots were heard, and Messrs. Oliphant and Morrison appeared deluged with blood. Tho assassins were in the house, and, with the exception of Mr. Morrison, no one of us had firearms ready. After a brief pause there was a renewal of the uproar, accompanied by smashing of glass and breaking of wood. The assassins were in tho next apartment, we being in Mr. þÿAlcock room. s By this time our guns were loaded. The yacunins now fell upon the ma rauders, and a great fight took place to in the tho ex tensive gardens and avenne leading river, the watchmen striking their two bits of wood in ment rapid time. lanterns with The yacunins rushed into our apart- and drawn swords, saying, penese þÿ Nipon yacunin þÿ! to muskets soldiers with let us know them. Ja- and fixed bayonets also entered aud went into tho garden, where they piled arms. Lanterns appeared iu all directions, and bonfires were made. The garden and park looked like a scene in a play. The fine, soldierlike Japanese guard being seen iu dim outlino grouped in different directions, before us a sheet ol water reflecting fires, lan-

terDS, and men, was a scene never to be forgotten, and even at the moment filled me with admiration. There was another alarm, and at the sound of the þÿwatchman rattle s the squatting groups jumped up, and wo stood to our arms. A yacunin and several soldiers rushed in out of breath and spotted with blood ; auother assassin j had been caught ; five of them were dead, and seven severely wounded. Wo listened anxiously to every sound. We could not walk two steps without four or five yacunins following us to i protect us. Search was made round the house for hidden assassins. Mr. Alcock was just going to sit in his easy-cliair when a pool of blood in the seat was pointed out to him ; Mr. Olipliant lay on the floor, with a mosquito-net over him, faint, and weak from loss of blood ; Mr. þÿMorrison wound s was ouly slight þÿ a cut in the forehead ; he stood with his sword in one hand, and a revolver in the other. So passed the night. Two of the g utlcnien lived in a little house further up the hill ; wo were very anxious about them, but gratified by seeing them join us safe and sound : they had not been disturbed. In the morning we went round to sec the grounds; they were filled with troops and the wildest-looking watchmen or policemen I ever saw, in all kinds of groups, on the grass; whilst here and there lay a ghastly mangled human form, one or two with their heads cut almost in two. The yacunins fought like tigers for us, and deserve all praise Mr. Alcock and M. do Bellecour went round to sec the wounded yacu-

nins. One had died ; the others were cut about, - but seemed quite cheerful, and gracefully bowed to Mr. Alcock and M. dc Bellecour in return for his thanks to them. They showed us their wounds and their notched swords, a sign that it was no þÿchild play. s One of them had a chainmail fillet cut in two on his head. The shavenheaded doctors were scientifically attending them, binding and bathing their wounds. How proudly the unwoundod walked þÿ in regular swash-buckler style, hand on the hilt of the sword, head erect, and eyes sparkling ! All the officers wear knickerbockers on these occasions. Early in the morning a courier was dispatched for the Ringdove, which vessel came up, bringing us a guard of marines and Freuchmen. The Ministers (Japanese) came at five in the morning, but did not get an audience till twelve þÿo clock at noon. Seven or eight of our yacunins were wounded. Three of the loonius committed suicide at Sinagawa next day, and another has been caught since, but notbiug certain is known as to who sent them. Prince Mito is reported to be the man, and the reason for their attacking only tho British Legation is said to be, not from any dislike to foreigners, but to involve the present Japanese Government in a war with England; for Mito was always trying to upset the present rulers, even before foreigners came. I have sent several Sketches with this letter. I hope next mail to send you an account of our journey through the interior.

Obituary. Died in tbe town of Frederiksted ou Friday night, the 15th inst., Revd. J. G. Pfannkr, Rector of tho Roman Catholic Church in that town. The deceased, although having been hut a year in this Island, had already won the respect and esteem not only of his parishioners hut of a large number of individuals of other denominations. His remains were interred on the following day, with all the soul-moving solemnities of his Church ; and followed by a large number of sorrowing friends and acquaintances, among whom, not the stoutest heart could avoid the shedding of a tear over the grave of him whom they had so soon learnt to love.

This morning (Saturday) the ears of those who already knew of, and of those who only anticipated it, tingled with the sound of the bell at the Roman Catholic Church announcing the death of the Reverend John Gregor Pfannicr, the parishpriest, after a very short illness. The reverend gentleman was horn in Alsace, France, in the year 1800. He came to this island in the middle of December last year, as successor to the late Rev. T. A. þÿO Ryan. þÿ Father þÿPlanner, though apparently disliked hy an insignificant party of his own congregation, created among the generality of the people of this town, general respect for his openness of manner and his unrestricted affability. The liberality and benevolence for which lie was remarkable, were unlimited save hy the hounds of necessary prudence ; his disinterestedness, his readiness to attend upon the sick and needy , were all qualities in the man praiseworthy, and met their reward here by the heart-expressing and expressed gratitude felt and poured forth, here and there, during his life-time, followed by general sym-

All these are demonstrations which serve to prove that, in some instances at least, merit has its immediate reward. In his capacity of priest the reverend Pfanner seemed to move among those of his flock, who, in my humble opinion, I believe qualified fo judge of their pastor, with ease and deference, lie was familiarly and respectfully addressed hy Protestant and Roman Catholics as þÿ father þÿPfanner. At Hie grave the address delivered hy the Reverend Mr. Lynch, was plain, unaffected, and touching. In a few words lie pictured out by negative comparisons, the solemnity of the occasion ; and hy a short hut direct and stirring appeal he spoke of the priest and the man, not with flattering encomiums hut hy a simple narration of facts. E V T B£ A C T Of a letter from a gentleman in Jamaica to a gentleman þÿ The Chinese immigrants, apart from their in St. Thomas. filthy and abominable habits ; are the least desirable class of laborers to introduce into a colony. In physical appearance they are before the Coolies : and about tho works of a sugar plantation are equally efficient, and, perhaps, more ingenious iu some respects ; hut for field work they are not so well adapted as the Coolies, as, besides otln r reasons, they are very subject, when so employ, d, to continual ulcers on their feet and legs, which so n renders them of little use. When their contract expires they almost universally flock to the towns, seldom, or never in fact, renewing it, or re-engaging for any kind of predial employment, while iu the towns to which they ro.-oit, especially in Kingston, they become a perfect nuisance as beggars, and the most expert thieves imaginable. The Coolies arc a docile, cleanly, and quiet people, much less refractory, and more ea-ily managed than the Chinese immigrants. Five hundred Japanese soldiers and 30 Marines from the flag-ship Impericuse form tho permanent guarJ, and three separate lines of palisades have been constructed round the temple which has hitherto formed tho abode of the British legation. It was the þÿAdmiral intention s to visit Ilakodadi, and then i rejoin the Impericuse at Yeddo. Tho Odin, Captain Lord John Hay, had left Nagasaki for Yeddo. Just as tlie French Government is announcing its intention to put down the course of anonymous pamphleteering, by which the ordinance requiring the signature of an author to his essay is eluded, anotlierampliLt is announced, as if tor the purpose of testing the resolution of the Minister of the Interior. In this instance, however, we think it will be quite unnecessary for the Fieneh Government to disavow any responsibility for the publication which is about to see the light under the rather multifarious title of England , Austria , and the.
