Prussia. The London morning papers have been full of the recent ceremonial of the Coronation of the King of Prussia at Konigsberg. The entry on their return of the King and Queen of Prussia into Berlin was announced by salutes of ar- , tillery and the pealing of hells. The streets from the Frankfort Gate to the Royal Palace presented a most festive appearance, all the houses being richly decorated, and the roadway bordered by Venetian masts. Their Majesties were evidently gratified at their reception, and cordially bowed their thanks to the people. Much distrust and dissatisfaction has been evoked in Germany, and indignation in this country, by the declaration of his Majesty, in putting the crown on his head, that he holds it from God alone. It is looked upon as a defiance of the progressive and Liberal party in Prussia, hut he alone will he the victim to such an absurd doctrine if lie conducts his future reign in the spirit thereof, unless all past history is to he reversed in the case of Prussia. Unhappily the coronation ceremonies have not

The intelligence as it now continues to reach i us from the United States, presents on every j occasion greater evidence of the final success of j the Federal Government over the rebellious States. By the last news we learn that the flag of the Union flies once more on the soil of South Carolina ; that a portion of the Navy octhe important harbour of Port Royal, and that the Military has the command of the district of Beaufort and is in possession of the railway that unites Charleston with Savannah. This recent conquest effects an important change in the relations of the contending forces ; J and already we hear that the rebels, alarmed at the safety of the remaining Southern Coasts, have detailed Beaurec.ard to take command there, by which means their Army in Virginia is deprived of its ablest soldier. In less than two weeks from the occupation of Beaufort it is thought that the Federal Government will have a force of not less than 50,000 men there, and by now a Custom House is opened at Port Royal for the benefit of all loyal citizens who may choose to bring their cotton for exportation to that quarter. Next in importance to the Federal Arms is, that Beaufort, with a cultivated area of some 250,000 acres, has a population of a little more than 32,000 slaves, which in a moment of extremity can be converted into as many lucifers. With Beaufort as a base, and an army of 50,000 men to be easily reinforced from Annopolis and Fortress Muuroe, it is thought that Charleston and Savannah, attacked

in the rear by the Army, and their sea defences attacked at the same time by the Navy, with a divided opinion (loyal and secession) in their midst, can hardly be expected to hold their own for any great while Regarding the foreign relations of the United States, the New York Herald of the 16th announces, in an editorial, that Mr. Motley, the American Minister accredited to Vienna, during his stay in London dined with Lord Palmerstox and Earl Russell, and both had informed him that the British Government had no intention of recognising the Confederate States be they were first recognised by the United States, or that it was clear to the world that the Federal Government was unable to quell the rebellion ; as well as it was not the intention of their Government to interfere with the blockade of the Southern ports. If this intelligence proves true, coupled with the events at Beaufort, the opinion might be hazarded that the rebellion has seen its best days.

AUSTRIA. The Emperor of Austria is hurrying on to try the great experiment whether six millions of Germans can hold in subjection thirty millions of other races by mere brute force. The Croatian Diet has been dissolved ; a special Aulic Chancellerie has been constituted at Vienna, and this distant province is to be directly governed from the capital of the German Archduchy. The consequence, of course, is that Croatia has been united to Hungary by Austria for all purposes of hatred to her rule. Austria gained her territories by happy alliances among her friends, and, false to all her traditions, she hopes to keep them by allying all her enemies against her. This wild and mountainous province of Croatia, with its ignorant, bigoted, and

$ Tu P R (L (! & li $5 barbarous population, and with its valuable outlet to the Adriatic, was of immense importance to Austria. It gave her soldiers whom she ci uld depend upon, arid gave her an enemy to the Hungarians in a province which was nominally an integral portion of the Hungarian how had already experienced kingdom. She decisive the action of tlie Croatian people might be in a great crisis, and, if there was any portion of that great Austrian Empire that ought at any price to be retained faithful to the House of Hapsburg, it certainly should have been that hill country where a population of Sclaves presses upon the side of the Magyars and holds the outlet to the sea. Croatia has not forgotten that she was once a kingdom holding dominion herself over neighbouring provinces. She has enjoyed immemorial privileges apart from Hungary, and she has always been as tenacious of them as any Hungarian noble could be of his. She is as proud, also, of her barbarous dialect as if it were the purest Saxon or the softest Tuscan, and when she sent deputies to the Hungarian Diet the attempted suppression of this dialect in the Croatian Courts was the cause of fierce hatred against the domineering Magyars. Such aie the people whom the young Emperor has just chosen to add to his list of open enemies. To spectators from a distance this conduct seems to deserve the name, not of policy, but of madness. We have heard of men who, when, they had a monitory twinge of gout, have swallowed two bottles of port

in order to bring it out in full development at once. But we must suppose these impatient victims to be confident in their remedies. They must be convinced that the enemy, when fully brought forth, will certainly yield before their stock of colcliicuin and flannels, and that there is no possibility ol its reaching the heart. Francis Joseph luis not even the excuse of the gouty man for his rash, heroic style, of treatment 'lhi Imperial corpus which Francis Joseph personates is not suffering from monitory twinges, but is already in full fit. Hungary is already swollen and painful, Poland vibrates with an angry throbbing, and Vcuetia is scarcely visible under her bandages. There cannot be any reason why he should swallow any more of his own constitutions in order to bring out Croatia. If he goes on thus, there will be no other place where a new accumulation of gout can take refuge except in the very heart of the Empire. But when he has succeeded and produced an universality of angry humours all over the kingdoms subject to Austria how does he propose to mluy them ? Where are his remedies? He has but one nostrum. Soldiers, gnu shot wounds, and bayonet thrusts are all he can trust to as a form of treatment. These are excellent expedients for destroying a country, but very bad means for governing one. These mighty armies are very certain agencies for eating up taxes, but very clumsy contrivances for collecting tliein. In a few years they can render even a country 1,000 miles by 500

utterly incapable of yielding any revenue ; but we never heard that they could so foster industry, manufactures, agriculture, and commerce that wealth should flow in rivers through the land. In the good old days when Austria had only a hundred millions of debt, and always got her thirteen milions paid into her exchequer, it was as ntuch as she could manage to keep her 300,000 men in a sufficient state of wooden discipline to punish rebellious peasants and to be beaten by any active, well equipped enemy. Under the most prosperous circumstances, with Russia free to come down to her assistance, and

ready to do so, it was hard work that governing by the sword. But now, when her credit is gone, when her old patron is not only sulky, but unable to move; when she has an open enemy with at least 100,000 good soldiers on her Southern frontier, and a very ambiguous friend separated from her only by some strips of land on her West, þÿ now, when site has neither money nor credit, and when her territories are the dread and despair of the traveller who has to change his good gold into flimsy rags, which are of only half their nominal value even in their own country, and þÿ the frontier, now, when she can only are of no value at a:! across maintain her soldiery by billeting them upon her subjects as in an enemy's country, þÿ now, when all these things have come upon h r, what can she mean by this ostentatious resolution to govern henceforward by the sword? The experiment of governing by the sword, to be successful, ought to be made by a very rich despot or upon a very rich country. It should be made by a conqueror who has the means of paying, and supplying an army of occupation, or in a country where the soldiers can find a living for themselves In tlio first case there may be hope that, after much treasure spent, the yoke may be riveted firmly ; in 'he second it may be expected that the cowardice of wealth may induce submission. The Emperor of Austria, however, lias neither of these advantages. Austria Proper has neither the money nor the credit to play the part of Venice in old days, and pay for

armies to hold a wi !e dominion far away. The provinces of Austria are not rich enough to support perpetually soldiers to keep populations of en nties in subjection. These popula'ions may suffer, but the soldiers will suffer also When the locusts .has overspread a co lit i y the husbandman sta ves, but lite locust also di s ; and the land is b asted not so much by the loss of the fruits of t li earth which the locust eats as by the cultivation it destroys. Of course, we say nothing about the morality of tins new resolve to reduce all Austian subjects to one level of unprivileged and rightless Austrians, ami to fule them by t lie sword. We submit that it cannot be done. Our first objection has been that it can never pay. But, even if this insuperable difficulty could bigot over, there is another. We nut aside the strong chance of any successful rising among the people. Without considering that, we see another fatal difficulty, þÿ the whole of this despotism must rest upon the single support of military di-cipline. The discipline, moreover, is to hold its influence over inert who are for the most part forced as conscripts from those very masses of population which are raging under the weight of military rule. They are taken away, too, just at the age when their sympathies are likely to bo in full blow. The young man, for instance, who was murdered the other day by the Austrian officers at Vicenza would, in all probability, if ho had lived, have been draughted into an Austrian regiment.

The natural expedient is to send the Hungarians to keep down the Croats and the Poles, and to quarter the Poles upon the Hungarians, and so on through all the counterchanges. It is a clever arrangement, and may answer so long as there are well-affected, loyal populations, left to furnish recruits enough to give a general tone to the army ; but the Emperor of Austria seems resolved that beyond the limits of the old Archduchy there shall not be a people who does not feel itself in some way wronged. The men in white coats and the men in blue tight panta-

loons, drill theiri as you may, are all iiems of these very populations. We notice it as a significant fact that the Hungarians and Croats now in Venetia have lost the slight distinctions which formerly existed in their uniforms, and the Venetians say this was done lhat the people might not count upon the sympathy of a Hungarian soldier. The last measure of the Emperor seems to tend towards rendering this amalgamation useless, and destroying the terrors of even a Croat soldier. We doubt whether even military discipline is, under such circumstances, to be relied upon as the only sheet anchor to prevent a great vessel like Austria from drifting upon the rocks- Suppose anything should happen to the army while this experiment is being worked out. It would bit a terrible collapse, and a great misfortune to Europe. It would be like a stone in a heavilyweighted arch tumbling out. This mad young Emperor litis something more than his own fate at stake, for, if Austria were to collapse and fall, all Europe's horses and all Europe's men could never put the Empire of Austria together again. þÿ London Times.

THE SUMTER IN MARTINIQUE. On Thursday the 14th, between 2 and 3 o'clock just as the Sumter had finished coaling and was making preparations to start, a large Steamer was signalised in sight, at the point du Precheur. In a moment the news spicad that a Federal Ship of War had come to fight with the Southern privateer at anchor in our harbour. Everyone knows the effect of any extraordinary news upon our population; immediately all the town carried itself to the beach, and the Place Berlin ; shops, counteis, houses, cveryp'ace was deserted, and it was necessary to go back to the famous engagement of the Cygne, which took place before the eyes of the people in 1809, to find an instance of an event as interesting as that of which we were about to become witnesses. In the mean timo the Steamer in sight approached Southern to her with a speed which augured no good adversary. Only a Danish flag hoisted at the gaff left in doubt if wo were in truth in presence of a Federal vessel. We were not kept long in suspense. As soou a9 the boats which had left the harbor, boarded the Steamer on her approach, and she was acquainted with the fact of the presenco of her enemy, the colors of the United States were immediately hoisted, and the Danish flag lowered. This ruse seems to have been resorted to, to prevent the Iroquois, which in-

$ t Sim & I S tended to go on to Fort de France, where she expected to meet the Sumter, from beiDg signalised by some of the signal posts, and the latter should have time to escape. In fine, in a few moments the Federal frigate was in the centre of the harbour, and to leave no doubt of her intentions, placed herself boldly before tbe Sumter, to whom her appearance could not have been very agreeable. The joy of the American crews and prisoners set on shore by the Sumter was great. They were seen in agitated groups passing along, happy without doubt to behold a flag to protect them, and probably likewise at being revenged upon, and relieved of their terrible visitor. Having communicated with the shore, the Iroquois asked permission to lie alongside of her adversary ; but this demand could not be admitted, first, because Ships of War have a particular anchorage assigned them, and further for this reason, because the neutrality of our Government made it our duty to remove as far as possible the chances of a conflict, the result of which could not be doubtful, looking at the guns and equipment of the Iroquois. As for the latter, she continues to keep her steam up within a short distance of ihc Sumter, and already for the last 24 hours, we have been watching with mingled anxiety aud confidence this reudesvous so lull of interest, that fi Is our mind with apprehension, if the Sumter will be able to escape from the Iroquois By means of some stratagem, aud tliro' his boldness, will her Captain renew the well known ante-

cedents of Jean Bart, Surcouf, and other bold privateers. When we remember the success with which he has hitherto eseap.d the' vigilance of the Federal cruisers, wo arc drawn into the most extravagant visi'iis of a thousand sclie'tnes by which the Iroquois will find herself seirne fine morning left alone in tho harbor a little ashamed, and not a little surprised. Ainoug-t the plans put forwatd, one of the most odious is, for the Sumter to take advantage of the night to escape Unfortunately the inoon disturbs this caleu'ation, and uulcss thro' the intervention of seine unexpected circumstance, wo cannot see before vessel can avoid considerable risk, how this a more perfect darkness comes to assist in her deliverance. We cannot expect to wait much longer fur the result of the challenge which for the last two days her formidable antagonist lying iu front of her, has given the Sumter like an enormous cat watching a mouse. Wc forgot to mention that a great number of persons expected a naval engagement in sight of our harbor. They imagined simply that the Sumter would attempt to force the blockade kept over her, and having got beyoud the neutral limit, the two enemies would tiro away at each other iu the opon sea, to tho great amusement of the spectators. But tho Sumter is not sent to fight with the chances against her ; she has orders on tho contrary to avoid every useless encounter, and if wo can credit the statements of those who have been on board the Iroquois, the disproportion

of strength would leave no hope to her adversary. At the moment at which we write these lines, tho French steamer Acheron, commanded by our countryman, M. Duebatul, has cast author iu the harbor. Pel haps he comes to act the pari of tho Dcus ex machiiui. In all probability our bravo countryman has been instructed to prcv nt an engagement between the two American vessels in the waters of St. Pierre, and to keep tho non. We aie unwilling to report Iroquois at a respectful distance from all In that r can- we hear talked about. In a few days we shall know the result. Whether the Sumter, as people say, will attempt an c-cape, or whether she will remain in complete inaction and leavo her adversary time to use his strength, þÿ we cannot say þÿ but what wo do say is, that our flag will be respected, and we cannot give too much praise to the energy of tho Governor of tiie Colony, who has lost no time to place tho Acheron between the two enemies, in order to keep them from coming to blows, if it is possible, and in any case to protect our harbor. For ourselves as neutrals we take no part one way or the other, for or against tho once united but now dis-unitcd States, but offer our best wishes that the courage and boldness exhibited so often by tho Sumter might not be unrewarded iu a well-conducted enterprise, iu which tho lives of so many bravo young men

''Lieutenant Warley had orders from Connno dore Hollius to run ahead of the whole expedition and make a trial of the ram under any circumstances and at all hazards. Her 9-inch gun was not to be used at all, and, in fact, she only had a dozen cartridges for it in her magazine. The porthole forward was closed down, and so was the after hatch. The forward hatch alone was opened four inches, so as to permit the steersman and pilot to have a good view ahead. Mr. Austin, who knows every inch of the river, piloted her himself, the pilot having left her at the fort. It was a peculiar hazard, this, to try a new invention without a preccdeut on which to form even a conjecture as to the result, and to run boldly into the midst of an enemy's fleet on the literal principle of 'Victory or death.' The men aboard of her were not Lightened, or they would not have deliberately made the venture, but tbey would not have been human if they had not felt the oppression of an awful suspense. Shut up in that ironbound case, they knew that in a short time it might be their coffin. It was pitch dark. for better night could not have been selected A the purpose, and the ram glided noiselessly down the current. Never before had she run so well. Ten miles an hour was supposed to be her maximum speed, but she was making at least 13 knots. The water ran up over her t>w, and split oft' on each side with beautiful play, making a gentle and really musical rippling sound. She had left the other boats far

behind, but still she kept on her swift course. All of a sudden Austin discovered the dim outlino of a ship right ahead. He sang out to tho engineer, 'Let her out, Hardy ; let her out now.' Instantly the tar, tallow and sulphur that had been prepared were thrown iDto her furnace, and the hand of her steam-gauge ran up to the highest point. How much pressure on the boilers was given can never be known, but it was far above her allowance. Now she was discovered by the watch on the enemy's decks, and they gave the alarm, and sent up a blue light from tho Richmond þÿ probably a privato signal to the Niagara below. Austin made out the bow of the vessel she was approachiog, and steered her for it so as to strike between her hog chains and main chains. The aim was a true one; the momentum of the ram was terrific, and the crash, as she drove her prow 20 feet Every deep into the ship's hull, was truly knocked man on board the Manassas was fearful. down by the violence of the concussion, and the wholo boat vibrated like an aspen. The engines were at once reversed, and she backed right out, bringing off on her prow whole sheets of of her Treble's coppering, and big splinters tho solid, live-oak bow. The dismay, the consternation, the panic of horror that ensued upon tho deck of the stricken Preble may bo imagined, but it cannot bo pictured in words. Most of the crew, aroused front slumbor, rushed frantically about, crazy with fright. Some of them must have been wounded and maDgled by tbe

sharp prow of the Manassas, judging from their piercing, agonising shrieks. A few of thorn were seen to leap overboard into the river, and upon deck a perfect saturnalia of frenzied terror reigned They knew not what was to follow, and could not understand what had occurred. In the Manassas their yells were distinctly heard, with such cries as, 'We're sinking !' 'She's going to blow up!' 'We're all lost.' 'Oh my God!' Tho Richmond, Yincennes, Preble, and Water Witch were at anchor in the line of a V, with spring cables, and steam up on the two steamers. As tho Manassas backed off from the Preble her officers saw tho Richmond lying right beforo them, with her full broadside exposed. Here was a splendid opsuccess portunity, and the against tlicy bad no doubt, from their Preble, that they would cut her in two. Not a single shot had been fired at them yet, and such was tho confusion on board

all of the ships that they commenced ringing their fog-bells, which proved that even yet they were so confused and ignorant of the nature of our attack that some of them supposed it to be an accidental collision, caused by tlfe extreme darkness, and rang the fog-bells, t o as to show the Manassas their position and enable her to avoid them. Again Mr. Austin sang out to the j engiueer, 'Now let ber out, Hardy, and give it to her.' It was at this moment that Mr. Hardy 1 discovered that one ol the condensers had been brokeu by the shock of the concussion in striking the Preble, which rendered had giues useless, and he knew she one of her en- not power i enough iu the other to run her into anything else. He therefore passed the word up that the machinery was disabled, and all she could do would be to haul off as best she could. Bitter was this disappointment to Lieutenant Warley, as ho saw the lull side of the Richmond right before him ; hut there was no help lor it, aud it might even bo a critical matter to escape. Working one engine she made a circuit her around to head up stream, and this brought right under the Richmond and the Vincenius. By this time the cfiieers on board those vessels had recovered their presence of mind sufficiently to j comprehend that this extraordinary collision j was no accident, but a very cool and audacious assaukt by the enemy, and that the long, low, black-locking object 'floating right before Then was the cause of their danger and alarm. them they manned their guns, which were already

shotted, and now the invulnerability of the Manassas was fairly tested. First came the whole broadside of the Richmond, and directly after the entire broadside of the A inccnnes, followed by the 8- inch shells of the Water AY itch. I he roar of cannon was tremendous, and it seemed to those cooped up in the little ram as if all the thuudorbolts of Jove were rained upon them. The flagstaff and one of the chimney-stacks of the Manassas were cut off as clean as il by a knife ; but the guns of the ships had not been sufficiently depressed, and all their balls except two or three went over her. She has arm- one indentation, near the bow, iu licr iron but our, to show that she was struck at all, but it is believed that other shots reached her and glanced off withouy leaving a perceptible mark of their visit. Now the confidence of all on board returned, and, after having passed through such a volley unseated, they kucw they were safe and souud.''

Tlic West Coast of Africa. DISCOVERY OF I) 11. BAIKIE. ANOTHER DAHOMEY MASSACRE. The Royal Mail steam-ship Ethiope, with the above mails, arrived at Liverpool on Saturday afternoon, after a very rapid passage from the West Coast. By this arrival we are placed in possession of news of the longlost African explorer, Dr. Baikie, regarding whose fate there has been so much speculation. It will he remembered that Dr. Baikie was attached for some time to the Niger expedition, and the last heard from him þÿ until the present time þÿ was upwards of two years ago. Since then the fate of himself and his assistant was a mystery, hut it was generally believed that he had either perished from the sickness and fatigue incident on his explorations, or that he had fallen a victim to some of the savage tribes of the country. We are, however, glad to say that the adventurous explorer and his assistant have at last been discovered alive and well, after a residence of two years amongst the natives, daring which time they were without communication with Europeans. During his two years' sojourn among the natives the Doctor enjoyed tolerably good health, and had likewise made some interesting researches in connection with the exploration of the Niger. The last advices left Dr. Baikie at the confluence of the river. The exploring steamer Sunbeam, and

T', M J I. A . V I . Sthe other vessels engaged in the expedition, had returned to the mouth of the Niger, after having been up to the confluence. Her Majesty's ship Fspour accompanied the vessels for protection, after which she sailed for the Island of Ascension. Another of those diabolical massacres which are a stigma on civilisation was about to be carried into effect tit Dahomey. The Canilml King was going to have another "grand custom." This sacrifice is to celebrate the new yam season, and the preparations were to have been of the most complete character. All the principal natives and traders at Lagos had received invitations to be present to witness the ceremony of cutting off the heads of about 2,000 human beings. From this il would appear that the protest lately made oinst such acts of barbarism by lit Jiritislt Government, through the late Air. Consul Foote, has had no effect on the King of Dahomey, and the general opinion appears to he that until "His Majesty" is disposed of by summary or other means, this reign of terror will not abate. The cultivation of the country around Dahomey, down to the very sea-board, was neglected, in consequence of the observance of the cruelties. Hunting parties had been sent out, to capture from neighbouring tribes the unhappy victims for the sacrifices. From Lagos we learn that a report was very prevalent at that place that the ex-King Dosomu had mustered about 2,000 natives under arms, for the purpose of taking the Acting Governor of Lagos, Commander Bedingfield, R. N.,

prisoner, and massncrcing the merchants. The plot, however, had explored, and the ex-King was said to have vanished. The King (Fepple) of Bonny was still on board his vessel, the Bowlah, in the Bonny river. His subjects were equally divided, some ready to support his being reinstated; others, and powerful chiefs, determined to oppose him. The following declaration had been signed by those chiefs who offer their aid in again placing him on the throne: þÿ "VVethc undersigned chiefs, and the people of the Bonny dominions, on behalf ofourselves, our heirs and successors, and of any chief or chiefs hereafter to he appointed, do hereby declare that we have no right, litle, or claim to the revenues, sovereignty, or Government, past, present, or future, of the said Bonny dominions, and do declare that the King William Pepple alone, and no other person or persons whomsoever, is our rightful Sovereign, and that we do not nor will accept or recognise any other person than the said King (and his rightful heirs after him) to be Sovereign of the said Bonny dominions, and that the said King has the sole and exclusive right, at all times and from time to time, to receive all revenue, and to make and carry into effect such good and useful laws and regulations for the rule and management of the coir try, and to make treaties with any foreign Power, as he may deem expedient. Done at Bonny this 24th day of August, in the year of our Lord 18(51." The people brought out by the King of Bonny from England are tired and

disgusted with the expedition, and anxious to leave him. Many have already done so. Her Majesty's ship Bloodhound paid a visit to the river, at the request of the English traders, to protect the British interests, in case of a civil war between the two parties. News had reached Fernando I'o of an English vessel having gone ashore in

the Congo river, and been totally plundered by the natives. A British war vessel had gone round to the place. An Englishman named Lee was missing at Fernando Po. He was supposed to have been killed by the Boobies, as his clothes and jewellery had been traced. A strict investigation would he held by the English consul. The island was healthy. News from the Gold Coast stales that Governor Andrews has had several ol the native chiefs from the Crobboe country seized and imprisoned in the fort, where they arc to remain until the fine imposed upon them after the late war to is paid. The governor is endeavouring organise another expedition against some of the tribes in the interior, and has been nntking application to Her Majesty's cruisers for a naval brigade. Serious disturbances exist in the protectorate in consequence of the poll tax, which the natives consider unjust and oppressive, and which they are determined to resist. Large quantities of oil were coming forward, and trade was better thiin has been known for some y tars. þÿ London Paper.

Destruction of a Bridc.e near Rome. þÿ An eye-witness gives ihe following account of the destruction of the magnificent midge at Civita Castcllaoa, 40 miles from Rome, which traversed the ravine, at tlio en ry of that town from Narni, at a height of 120ft. above the torrent, and was constructed upon more ancient foundations hy Cardinal Imperial-! in 1712, in the reign of I'ope Clement XL; þÿ "You are doubtless aware of tiic tremendous rains aud the daintgo produced hy them here in Civita Castellana ou the 29:h and 30th of October. There are in our territory three important bridges, among which is t lie reuo vned ouc known as the Clementine, close to the city, which Napoleon I. declared to be the best work of the kind in Italy. It was extremely lofty, supported on five pila.-tirs of grandiose dimensions. These tln\c bridges, struck by the impetus of the waters after midday on the 30th ult , were all carried away. Ou that morning the Clcmentino-bridge was visit, d by numerous spectators, curious to behold the increase aud the violence of the rushing element below. About 3 p.m. I also, accompanied by iny friend. Signer Ferdinando O , repaired to the the bridge to gaze upon the bead- long course of swollen torrent. We stopped to look over fruni the pr j cting recess on the centre of the bridge to lite tight band. At that moment the handle of the umbrella which 1 carried in my hand got entangled in my coat; I turned round to disentangle it, and, in so doing, I saw the wall of the recess in the act of

splitting I is shiutcd out to G the bridge falling!' AVe fled as last as our , 'Escape, for feet would carry us, and were still on the last arch but one when the bridge began to give way at the centre recess, where we had been standing, and continued falling in the direction of the city, towards which we had fled, so that- we saved our lives by having a start of 10 or la! yards. The catastrophe produced the greatest consternation in Civita Castellana, it being tear, d that a great many persons had been precipitated iuto the current; but 1 was able to calm the general apprehension by the assurance that my friend and myself -were the only two persons on the' bridge at the time. It is a terrible thing to see laid low a biidge which, from its appearance, promised an almost eternal duration. Only one pilaster is still upright, the lust on the Narni side, which also I distinct ly saw oscillate twice after it lost the support of the other masonry. It now seems flint again AVe have an inspector and some engineers here, aud a new supplementary road is already being commenced on a convenient track by Santa Maria (the ancient Etruscan city of Phalleri), which we hope will be completed in about a month." The road alluded to will cross tlie torrent and ravine about four miles higher up, and so reopen the communication between Rome and the province of Umbria. In the present session of the Colonial Council, a draft of a biennial budget for the Westindia Possessions, for the years from 1st April 1862 to 31st March 1864, has, for the first time, been laid before the Council, no budget, for the present year, again having been laid hefore the Council. The more therefore does the Council feel itself called upon to examine the relations under which the Colonial Council is placed, and to endeavour to prevent that the removal of an irregular state of things and of unbearable burthens which now press upon the islands be postponed until 1864, after a discussion in a next meeting of the Imperial Council (in the autumn 1863. 2. The Draft of Budget concerns, so as the former budgets, the revenue and expenditure of the 3 islands, but merely as one Chapter of the revenue and expenditure of the danisli state during the financial period. The action of the local representation with regard to a budget so constituted, would consistently tend not to a favorable result for the Treasury, but to the very reverse thereof, namely to secure the greatest possible outlay in the island, and the smallest possible reveuue therefrom. Discussions on such estimates can never be satisfactory ; still for want of something Letter, they might be of some use, as long as the Colonial- Council was summoned regularly, all the islands were represented iu the same : aud the confidence of obtaining some result, or in the initiative of Government, bad not been weak-

ened. But, leaving alone the other matters, since 1854 the island of jjt. Thomas has not been represented at the 2 (two) meetings held since that time ; nor has the Government for the present session effected elections for St. Thomas. Under such circumstances it is not considered advisable or fair towards the inhabitants of St. Thomas, for this Colonial Council again to give opinions on taxation or local measures and expenses in St. Thomas. Disregarding the question, whether publio arrangements with regard to taxation and representation suitable for St. Croix would also be satisfactory for St. Thomas, it is now placed beyond doubt, that the continuance of a Colonial Council, common for the islands only by name, would for St. Thomas he perfectly useless, and would as tar as St. Croix is concerned retain the appearance of certaiu public guarantees, but in reality conceal retrogression both in public affairs and in prosperity. The Colonial Council for the above reasons, considers it an indispensable condition for further necessary measures with regard to the settlement of all financial questions, that separato Colonial Councils be established for St. Croix and for St. Thomas and St. Johns, as provided by the first paragraph of the Colonial Law. A draft of an Ordinance to effect this, proposed by the members of the Committee that have treated the present draft, has been adopted by the Council, and copy of the same is attached as voucher No. 1. With regard to the contents we only deem it necessary to

observe, that if the increase of elected members. þÿ say 2 for St. Croix and 2 for St. Thomas and St. Johns þÿ which has been suggested as more conformable with the general tenor of the Colonial Law, which presupposes a not very small Assembly (20 members) þÿ should he considered as inconsistent with the tenor of C.
